section.title: The Death of Abraham
section.sectionRationale: Abraham's long life comes to its quiet, contented close. He settles his other children with gifts, gives all he has to Isaac, and dies full of years. Two estranged sons bury him together, and God's blessing passes on to Isaac, the promise still moving.
section.thesis: Abraham dies old and satisfied, his inheritance secured for Isaac and his blessing continuing; the man who lived by promise is gathered to his people in peace, and the covenant blessing flows on to the next generation.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: Abraham's other children provided for; the death and burial of Abraham; God's blessing passing to Isaac.

units.label: Abraham's other children
units.note: gifts to the sons of the concubines

verses.text: Now Abraham had taken another wife, named Keturah,
and she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Jokshan was the father of Sheba and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were the Asshurites, the Letushites, and the Leummites.
The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were descendants of Keturah.
Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac.
But while he was still alive, Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east.

units.label: The death and burial of Abraham
units.note: old and contented, gathered to his people

verses.text: Abraham lived a total of 175 years.
And at a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and {{contented|contented}}, and was {{gathered|gathered to his people}}.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite.
This was the field that Abraham had bought from the Hittites. Abraham was buried there with his wife Sarah.
After Abraham’s death, God {{barak|blessed}} his son Isaac, who lived near Beer-lahai-roi.

contented.gloss: Full, satisfied, having had enough. It describes a life lived to fullness and a soul at rest, not merely long years. Abraham dies satisfied, having seen God begin to keep His promises, a man who received the son of promise and could let go in peace.

gathered.gloss: To gather, collect, or take in. The phrase gathered to his people speaks of joining one's forefathers in death, and hints at a hope beyond the grave, that the dead are not lost but gathered. It is used of the peaceful passing of the patriarchs into the company of those who went before.

barak.gloss: To bless, to bestow favour and life giving good, from a root linked to kneeling. God's blessing is His active goodness that makes fruitful and prospers. Here the blessing that rested on Abraham passes to Isaac, so the covenant favour continues unbroken into the next generation.

basic.context: Abraham's story draws to a close. He has other sons through Keturah, but he provides for them with gifts and sends them east, while giving his whole inheritance to Isaac, the son of promise. He dies at 175, old and satisfied, and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael. The key question is how the promise continues past Abraham's death.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a historical summary that closes one era and opens another. It carefully distinguishes Isaac, the heir of the covenant, from Abraham's other children. The question is how the writer signals that God's promise is not tied to Abraham's life but flows on to Isaac by God's own choice and blessing.
basic.originalLanguages: Abraham dies sabea, full and contented, a life brought to satisfying completeness. He is gathered, asaph, to his people, a phrase hinting at hope beyond death. Then God blesses, barak, Isaac, so the covenant favour that rested on the father continues on the son.
basic.typology: Abraham dying in faith, satisfied though he saw only the first fruits of the promise, pictures all who die trusting God's word. The blessing passing to Isaac foreshadows the inheritance that comes to God's children in Christ, the true heir through whom the blessing reaches the world.
basic.christ: The blessing that flows from Abraham to Isaac runs on through the generations to Christ, in whom the promise to bless all nations is fulfilled. Abraham died satisfied by faith in what he could not yet fully see; in Christ the promise he trusted is brought to completion.
basic.god: God is faithful across a whole lifetime and beyond it. He blessed Abraham in every way, gave him a satisfying end, and then blessed Isaac, showing that His promise does not die with the patriarch. He is the God who gathers His people and carries His covenant forward.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 15 promised Abraham he would go to his fathers in peace at a good old age. Hebrews 11 says he died in faith. Galatians 3 says the blessing of Abraham comes to the nations in Christ. Matthew 22 calls God the God of the living.
basic.oneStory: Abraham dies full of years and faith, and the blessing passes to Isaac. The promise is bigger than any one life; it moves on through the covenant line, generation to generation, toward Christ, in whom the whole world is blessed.

context.literary:
These eleven verses close the account that opened at Genesis 11:27, 'This is the account of Terah.' Abraham has no toledot heading of his own; his whole story sits inside his father's. That account began with a death, 'Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran,' Genesis 11:32, and it ends with another, 'Abraham lived a total of 175 years,' verse 7. Between the two death notices stands the life of faith, and the frame is shaped to show it: Terah dies outside the land, Abraham dies inside it and is buried in ground he owns.

The passage has three short movements. First comes a genealogy, verses 1 to 4, sixteen names descended from Keturah across three generations. Then comes a settlement of the estate, verses 5 and 6, with a sharp contrast: to Isaac 'everything he owned,' to the other sons 'gifts,' and a sending 'away from his son Isaac.' Then comes the death and burial, verses 7 to 10, and a single closing verse on the blessing of Isaac, verse 11.

The order is theological, not chronological. Abraham was a hundred when Isaac was born, Genesis 21:5, so Isaac was seventy five at his father's death. Isaac was sixty when Jacob and Esau were born, Genesis 25:26, which means Abraham lived to see his grandsons reach fifteen. Genesis tells of Abraham's death before their birth so that his story is complete before the next one begins. The same pattern follows immediately: the line of Ishmael is closed off in verses 12 to 18, and only then does 'the account of Abraham's son Isaac' begin, verse 19.

The burial scene balances the story's tensions. Isaac and Ishmael, the two sons whose rivalry forced Hagar's expulsion in Genesis 21, stand together at the grave, verse 9. The cave is identified with legal precision, 'the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite,' 'the field that Abraham had bought,' verses 9 and 10, tying the end of Abraham's life to the deed of Genesis 23. The last word on Abraham's story is not his death but 'God blessed his son Isaac,' verse 11.
context.historical:
The names of Keturah's descendants point to peoples of Arabia and the desert fringes east and south of Canaan. Midian is the best known: the Midianites later appear in the Sinai and northwest Arabia, where Moses found refuge and married into the family of Jethro, 'the priest of Midian,' Exodus 2:15-21 and 18:1. Sheba and Dedan were trading peoples of Arabia, famed for caravans and goods, Ezekiel 27:20 and Isaiah 60:6. The same two names appear elsewhere in the Table of Nations under Cush, Genesis 10:7, which may reflect peoples whose connections and territories overlapped. Ephah, a son of Midian, is paired with Midian in Isaiah 60:6. Some connect the name Keturah with the word for incense, which would fit the incense routes these peoples controlled, but the link is uncertain.

The settlement of the estate fits what is known of ancient family practice. Sons of secondary wives might have claims on an inheritance, and a father could settle those claims by gifts during his lifetime, leaving the principal estate to the chief heir. Abraham does exactly this 'while he was still alive,' verse 6, so that there could be no contest after his death. Sending the other sons 'to the land of the east' also kept them from competing with Isaac for pasture and wells in Canaan.

The chronology is striking. Abraham had come to Canaan at seventy five, Genesis 12:4, and he died at a hundred and seventy five, so he lived exactly a century as a sojourner in the land of promise. Ishmael, born when Abraham was eighty six, Genesis 16:16, was then about eighty nine. Isaac was living near Beer-lahai-roi, verse 11, the well in the Negev between Kadesh and Bered where the angel had found Hagar, Genesis 16:14.
context.canonical:
Abraham's peaceful death is the exact fulfilment of Genesis 15:15, 'You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age.' The phrase 'at a ripe old age' in verse 8 is the same expression, and the Old Testament later gives it to a few others: Gideon, Judges 8:32, and David, 'He died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor,' 1 Chronicles 29:28. The death formula, breathing his last, dying, being gathered to his people, returns for Ishmael, Genesis 25:17, Isaac, Genesis 35:29, and Jacob, Genesis 49:33. Isaac's funeral mirrors Abraham's: two estranged brothers, Esau and Jacob, bury their father together, Genesis 35:29.

Keturah's sons show God's promise that Abraham would be 'the father of many nations,' Genesis 17:4-5, taking literal shape. Their later history is mixed. Midian gives Moses a home and a wise father in law, Exodus 18, but also leads Israel into sin at Peor, Numbers 25:16-18, and later oppresses Israel until Gideon's victory, which Isaiah remembers as 'the day of Midian,' Isaiah 9:4. Isaiah's vision of the end reverses the sending away: 'young camels of Midian and Ephah, and all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD,' Isaiah 60:6.

In the New Testament Abraham remains alive to God. Jesus says God 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Luke 20:38, speaks of Lazarus being carried 'to Abraham's side,' Luke 16:22, and of many who will come from east and west 'to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Matthew 8:11. Jesus also says, 'Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day,' John 8:56. Paul calls Abraham 'the father of us all,' Romans 4:16, and Hebrews says of him and his family, 'All these people died in faith,' Hebrews 11:13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to see how a life of faith ends. Abraham had lived a hundred years in the land as a foreigner, owning only a grave. He did not see his descendants multiply into a nation or take possession of Canaan. Yet he dies 'old and contented,' verse 8, exactly as God had promised in Genesis 15:15. Israel was to learn that the man who trusts God's promise can die satisfied before he sees it fulfilled.

He also meant Israel to know clearly who the heir was. Abraham had eight sons, Ishmael, Isaac and the six sons of Keturah, and Israel lived among the peoples descended from them. The chapter makes plain that 'Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac,' verse 5, and that the others were sent away with gifts. The line of promise ran through Isaac alone, by Abraham's deliberate act and by God's blessing, verse 11.

Finally, the author wanted Israel to see that God's blessing does not depend on any one man. The book has been focused on Abraham for fourteen chapters, and now he is gone. The single sentence 'God blessed his son Isaac' tells the reader that the promise has not died with him. The story of redemption is God's story, not Abraham's, and God carries it on.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes Abraham's marriages, his settlement of his estate and his funeral. It does not command a way of dividing an inheritance, and it does not approve having concubines, a practice Genesis records without endorsing and whose troubles it shows in the stories of Hagar and later of Jacob's wives.

What carries over is a pattern for ending well. Abraham puts his affairs in order while he is alive, verse 6, provides fairly for all his children, and makes his intentions clear so that there is no dispute after his death. That is wise stewardship in any age.

The deeper application is to the believer's death. Abraham dies satisfied because he trusts the promise, not because he has seen everything fulfilled. Hebrews holds him up as a model of dying in faith, Hebrews 11:13, and Paul could say, 'to die is gain,' Philippians 1:21. Christians face death with the same trust, now grounded in the resurrection of Christ, 1 Thessalonians 4:14.

debates.question: What does 'gathered to his people' imply about life after death?

views.label: A hint of continued existence with the ancestors
views.case: The phrase is separate from the burial, which comes afterward in verse 9, and Abraham's actual forebears were buried far away in Mesopotamia, Genesis 11:32. Moses is said to be 'gathered to your people,' Deuteronomy 32:50, though he was buried alone by God, Deuteronomy 34:6. The phrase therefore seems to describe joining the dead, not merely lying in a family tomb.

views.label: A dignified idiom for death
views.case: Others take it as a respectful expression for a peaceful death, like 'go to your fathers in peace,' Genesis 15:15, without a developed view of the afterlife. The Old Testament's picture of life after death grows only gradually, and it would be unwise to read too much into one idiom.

views.label: A seed that later revelation grows
views.case: A third view holds both together. The phrase implies that the dead are not simply gone, but its full meaning waits for later revelation, such as Daniel 12:2 and Jesus' own argument that God is 'the God of the living,' Luke 20:38.

debates.bearing: The third view is the most faithful. Genesis does not teach a detailed afterlife here, but it does distinguish being gathered from being buried, and the New Testament confirms that Abraham is alive to God, Luke 16:22 and Luke 20:37-38.

debates.question: When did Abraham take Keturah as his wife?

views.label: After Sarah's death
views.case: The passage follows Sarah's burial and Isaac's marriage, and the plainest reading is that Abraham remarried in his last decades. On this view his fathering six more sons after the age of 140 shows God's continued blessing and the reach of the promise that he would be 'a father of many nations,' Genesis 17:5.

views.label: Earlier, during Sarah's lifetime
views.case: The BSB renders verse 1 'had taken,' which allows an earlier time. Verse 6 speaks of Abraham's 'concubines' in the plural, and 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls Keturah 'Abraham's concubine,' suggesting she was a secondary wife alongside Sarah. Paul describes Abraham's body at about a hundred as 'decrepit,' Romans 4:19, and Hebrews 11:12 calls him 'as good as dead,' which some think makes many sons after 140 less likely.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the timing, and nothing depends on it. The narrator places Keturah here because this is where Abraham's estate is settled, and the point is the contrast between the many sons who receive gifts and the one son who receives everything.

debates.question: Does Isaac and Ishmael's joint burial of Abraham signal reconciliation?

views.label: A sign of healing
views.case: Ishmael had been sent away after mocking Isaac, Genesis 21:9-14, yet he returns to stand with Isaac at their father's grave, verse 9. Isaac, for his part, is living near Beer-lahai-roi, the well associated with Hagar, Genesis 16:14. Some see a quiet reconciliation between the brothers.

views.label: A customary duty
views.case: Others note that burying a father was a duty sons performed regardless of their relationship, and that the text says nothing about their feelings. The same thing happens when Esau and Jacob bury Isaac, Genesis 35:29, though their tensions were far from resolved.

debates.bearing: The text is restrained, but the picture of two estranged sons together at Abraham's grave is surely intended. Whatever their relationship, both are sons of Abraham and both receive a blessing from God, even though only one inherits the covenant.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'breathed his last' in verse 8 is gava, to expire or perish. It appears in the flood narrative, where 'every living thing that moved upon the earth perished,' Genesis 7:21, and God warns that everything 'will perish,' Genesis 6:17. In the patriarchal narratives it becomes part of a formal death notice, repeated for Ishmael, Genesis 25:17, Isaac, Genesis 35:29, and Jacob, Genesis 49:33. The same verb that describes death as judgment in the flood here describes a peaceful end, a small sign that death itself looks different for those who die in God's promise.

The phrase 'at a ripe old age' is literally 'in good grey hair,' beseivah tovah. The noun seivah means grey hair and so old age. It is the exact phrase God used in Genesis 15:15, making verse 8 a word for word fulfilment of that promise. Proverbs 16:31 says 'Gray hair is a crown of glory,' and Isaiah 46:4 has God promise to bear His people up 'when you turn gray.' Abraham's grey hair is a sign that God kept His word across the whole span of a life.

The word for 'contented' in the BSB, from the root saba, means to be satisfied or filled. Isaac's death notice uses the same word in a fuller phrase, 'old and full of years,' Genesis 35:29, and Job dies 'old and full of years,' Job 42:17. The sense is not merely that Abraham grew old but that his life reached its full measure. The same root describes the satisfaction God gives, as when the psalmist says, 'when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence,' Psalm 17:15.

The word for 'people' in 'gathered to his people' is the plural ammav, literally 'his peoples' or 'his kin.' The expression is used of Aaron, Numbers 20:24 and 26, and Moses, Deuteronomy 32:50, and a related phrase, 'gathered to their fathers,' is used of Joshua's generation, Judges 2:10.

Verse 6 speaks of 'the sons of his concubines,' using the plural pilagshim. The word describes a secondary wife, recognised but without the full standing of a primary wife. Verse 1 calls Keturah 'another wife,' but 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her 'Abraham's concubine,' so the plural in verse 6 probably includes both Hagar and Keturah.

The contrast in verses 5 and 6 turns on two phrases. Isaac receives 'everything he owned,' kol asher lo, the same phrase the servant used in Genesis 24:36. The other sons receive mattanot, 'gifts,' a word for presents given freely. The difference is between an inheritance and a gift. And the other sons are sent to 'the land of the east,' erets qedem. In Genesis the east is the direction of departure from blessing: the cherubim guard the east of Eden, Genesis 3:24, Cain settles east of Eden, Genesis 4:16, and Lot journeys east toward Sodom, Genesis 13:11. The 'people of the east' later appear in Judges 6:3 as raiders against Israel, and Job is 'the greatest man of all the people of the East,' Job 1:3.

Finally, verse 11 says that 'God blessed his son Isaac,' using barak with Elohim, the general name for God, as the subject. The same verb in Genesis 12:2-3 carried the promise to Abraham, and here it passes to Isaac.

typology.type: Isaac the sole heir who receives everything
typology.fulfillment: Abraham gives 'everything he owned to Isaac,' verse 5, while the other sons receive gifts. Hebrews says God has appointed His Son 'heir of all things,' Hebrews 1:2. The correspondence is a single heir at the centre of the father's purpose. The escalation is that Christ does not keep the inheritance to Himself; believers become 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17, and 'since you are a son, you are also an heir through God,' Galatians 4:7. The type falls short because Isaac's inheritance was flocks and silver, while Christ's is the whole creation, and those outside the covenant are brought into His inheritance rather than sent away.

typology.type: Abraham dying in faith and gathered to his people
typology.fulfillment: Abraham dies satisfied, trusting a promise he has not yet seen fulfilled, and is gathered to his people. Hebrews 11:13 reads his death as faith that greeted the promises from afar. Jesus later speaks of Lazarus carried by angels 'to Abraham's side,' Luke 16:22, and of Abraham alive in the kingdom, Luke 13:28. The escalation comes in Christ, who 'by His death' frees those 'held in slavery by their fear of death,' Hebrews 2:14-15. Abraham's peaceful death foreshadows the believer's; but unlike Abraham, the believer dies after the resurrection of Christ, knowing the promise has been sealed by an empty tomb.

typology.type: The sons of the east sent away with gifts
typology.fulfillment: Keturah's sons, including Midian, Ephah, Sheba and Dedan, are sent 'to the land of the east' with gifts, verse 6. Isaiah pictures their descendants coming back: 'young camels of Midian and Ephah, and all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense,' Isaiah 60:6. When Christ is born, 'Magi from the east' come to worship Him, Matthew 2:1, bringing 'gold and frankincense and myrrh,' Matthew 2:11. Matthew does not name them as Abraham's descendants, so this is an echo rather than a declared type. But the direction reverses: those once sent away from the heir now come east to west to bring gifts to the true Heir.

typology.type: Two estranged sons together at their father's grave
typology.fulfillment: Isaac and Ishmael, divided since Genesis 21, stand side by side to bury Abraham, verse 9. The picture is only a moment, and their descendants remain apart. In Christ the division between the covenant people and those outside is finally healed, for He 'has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14, creating 'one new man out of the two,' Ephesians 2:15. The escalation is from a shared grave to a shared life, and the type falls short because Abraham's sons met at a tomb, while Christ's people meet at a table, Matthew 8:11.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through the promise that runs through Isaac. Abraham gives everything to one son, verse 5, and God's blessing rests on that son, verse 11. Paul reads the promise to Abraham's offspring as narrowing to one person, 'and to your seed,' meaning One, who is Christ, Galatians 3:16. Matthew's Gospel opens, 'Abraham was the father of Isaac,' Matthew 1:2. The line that the passage protects is the line along which the Messiah will come.

It leads to Christ through the theme of the heir. Isaac, the son of promise, receives the whole inheritance. Hebrews says God has appointed His Son 'heir of all things,' Hebrews 1:2, and Paul makes the astonishing point that all who belong to Christ share that inheritance: 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise,' Galatians 3:29. The sons of Keturah were sent away with gifts. In Christ, those who were once outsiders are not merely given gifts; they become heirs.

It leads to Christ through Abraham's hope in the face of death. Abraham died without seeing the fulfilment, but Jesus says, 'Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad,' John 8:56. When challenged, Jesus answers, 'before Abraham was born, I am!' John 8:58. The one Abraham looked forward to was already the eternal Son. Jesus also argues from God's title 'the God of Abraham' that the dead are raised, Luke 20:37-38. Abraham's death is not the end of Abraham, because the God of Abraham is the God of the living, and the resurrection of Christ is the proof.

It leads to Christ by contrast. Abraham died 'old and contented,' surrounded by sons, at peace, gathered to his people. Jesus died young, rejected by His own people, crying out, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46. Abraham's death was full; Christ's was forsaken. Yet it is through Christ's forsaken death that His people can die as Abraham did, in peace. Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, prays, 'You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation,' Luke 2:29-30. Hebrews says Christ's death frees 'those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death,' Hebrews 2:15.

A caution is in order. Abraham's gifts, the land of the east and the details of his burial are not coded pictures of Christ. The links above rest on the promise and on the New Testament's own use of Abraham. What the passage gives is a model of dying in faith and a clear line of promise, both of which find their meaning in the One Abraham rejoiced to see.
study.god:
The passage shows God's faithfulness across a whole lifetime. Seventy five years before this, God called Abraham from Haran. Decades before, while Abraham was still childless, He promised, 'You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age,' Genesis 15:15. Now the narrator records Abraham's death in the same words. God does not forget a promise made decades earlier. Genesis 24:1 had already said that 'the LORD had blessed him in every way,' and verse 8 shows that blessing reaching all the way to the end.

God's faithfulness also extends beyond a single life. Abraham dies, but the promise does not. 'After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac,' verse 11. God was never Abraham's possession; Abraham was God's servant. The promise that was spoken to Abraham was always God's promise, and God carries it on to the next generation without interruption. Later He will speak to Isaac directly, 'I will be with you and bless you,' and 'I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham,' Genesis 26:3.

God shows His sovereign choice. The passage lists eight sons of Abraham, but only one inherits the covenant. That choice is not based on birth order, since Ishmael was older, or on number, since Keturah bore six. It rests on God's word, 'I will establish My covenant with Isaac,' Genesis 17:21. Paul later draws out this point, 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' Romans 9:7.

Yet God's kindness reaches beyond the chosen line. The sons of Keturah become peoples, as God promised when He made Abraham 'a father of many nations,' Genesis 17:5. Ishmael is present at the burial, a son God had blessed and promised to make fruitful, Genesis 17:20. God's electing love for Isaac does not mean indifference to the others.

God is also the God of the living. Abraham is 'gathered to his people,' not simply laid in the ground, and Jesus says of him, 'He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive,' Luke 20:38. Death is real, but it does not end God's relationship with those who trust Him.

For worship, the passage invites believers to trust God across the long span of their lives, and to face death as Abraham did, satisfied in God's faithfulness. It also invites them to thank God that His purposes do not depend on them. When they are gone, the God who blessed Isaac will go on blessing His people.

crossReferences.note: God promised, 'You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age.' Genesis 25:8 uses the same phrase for 'ripe old age.' Decades after the promise, given while Abraham was still childless, God keeps it to the letter, showing that His word holds across a whole lifetime.

God renamed Abram Abraham, saying, 'I have made you a father of many nations.' The six sons of Keturah and their descendants, listed in Genesis 25:1-4, together with Ishmael's twelve princes that follow, show that promise beginning to take literal shape.

Isaac 'breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of years. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.' The scene deliberately mirrors Abraham's death and burial, with two estranged sons again standing together at their father's grave.

God tells Moses he will die 'and be gathered to your people,' though Moses is later buried alone by God in an unknown place, Deuteronomy 34:6. This shows that being gathered to one's people is something other than burial in a family tomb.

Isaiah pictures 'young camels of Midian and Ephah, and all from Sheba' coming to Zion 'bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD.' The descendants of Keturah, sent away in Genesis 25:6, return in the age to come as worshippers.

Jesus says, 'many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.' Abraham, gathered to his people, is pictured as alive at the great feast, and those from the east are welcomed rather than sent away.

Jesus argues that because God calls Himself 'the God of Abraham,' the dead are raised, for 'He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.' Abraham, who died and was gathered to his people in Genesis 25:8, is alive to God.

Jesus says Abraham 'rejoiced that he would see My day,' and then declares, 'before Abraham was born, I am!' The one whom Abraham looked forward to, and who is the true Heir of the promise, existed before Abraham and outlives his death.

'All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised.' Abraham's death in Genesis 25:8 is the clearest example. He dies satisfied, though he has seen only a grave in the land and one son of promise.

God has appointed His Son 'heir of all things.' Abraham's gift of 'everything he owned' to Isaac, Genesis 25:5, anticipates the Father's appointment of the Son as heir, and through Him believers become co-heirs, Romans 8:17.

'If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise.' The inheritance that went to Isaac alone in Genesis 25:5 is opened in Christ to all who believe, so that outsiders become heirs rather than receiving only gifts.

study.oneStory:
At creation God gave humanity life and a world to inherit. At the fall death entered, and the refrain of Genesis 5, 'and then he died,' marked every generation. Abraham's death belongs to that same story. He too returns to the dust. Yet his death is different. He dies 'at a ripe old age,' 'old and contented,' 'gathered to his people,' verse 8, and he is buried in the land of promise. Death is still an enemy, but for the man of faith it has lost its terror.

The passage answers the question that has hung over Abraham's story since Genesis 12: will the promise survive him? God called Abraham to become a great nation and to bless all families of the earth, Genesis 12:2-3. Now he dies, having seen only one son of promise and one grave in the land. But the promise does not die with him. 'God blessed his son Isaac,' verse 11. Abraham's life closes and the story goes on.

The passage also sets up what follows. The sons of Keturah become peoples on Israel's borders, some friendly and some hostile. Ishmael's line is recorded next, Genesis 25:12-18, and then the story narrows to Isaac, his sons Jacob and Esau, and the choice of Jacob, Genesis 25:19-26. The promise continues to pass from one generation to the next, never secured by human strength and always carried by God's blessing.

In Christ the story comes to its centre. He is the seed of Abraham in whom the promise to bless all nations is fulfilled, Galatians 3:8 and 3:16. He is the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, and through Him believers from every nation become heirs as well, Galatians 3:29. His death and resurrection break the power of death, Hebrews 2:14-15, so that believers can die as Abraham did, in peace.

The new creation brings the final gathering. People will come 'from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God,' Luke 13:29, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The sons of the east who were sent away will come bringing gifts, Isaiah 60:6. And death, which Abraham met with contentment, will be no more, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: How did Abraham provide for his sons other than Isaac?

options.text: He gave them gifts and sent them away eastward, while leaving all his inheritance to Isaac.
options.note: Verses 5 and 6 distinguish the gifts to the other sons from the inheritance given to Isaac.

options.text: He divided his estate equally among all his sons.
options.note: He provides for them, but the inheritance goes to Isaac, not an equal division.

options.text: He left them nothing at all.
options.note: He does give them gifts; they are not left with nothing.

options.text: He sent them to live with Ishmael.
options.note: He sends them to the land of the east, not to Ishmael.

quiz.q: How does the text describe Abraham's death?

options.text: He died at a ripe old age, old and contented, and was gathered to his people.
options.note: Verse 8 pictures a full, peaceful, and satisfied death.

options.text: He died suddenly and unprepared.
options.note: The opposite; his death is peaceful and his affairs are settled.

options.text: He died grieving that he had seen none of God's promises.
options.note: He dies contented, having seen the promise begin in Isaac.

options.text: He died in battle defending his household.
options.note: There is no battle; he dies at a great age in peace.

options.text: Isaac and Ishmael together, in the cave of Machpelah he had bought.
options.note: Verses 9 and 10 record the two sons burying him in the purchased field.

options.text: Isaac alone, in a new tomb near Beersheba.
options.note: Isaac is involved, but Ishmael joins him, and the site is Machpelah, not a new tomb.

options.text: The Hittites, in one of their own tombs.
options.note: He is buried by his sons in the field he purchased from the Hittites, not in their tombs.

options.text: Keturah and her sons, in the land of the east.
options.note: It is Isaac and Ishmael who bury him, at Machpelah.

quiz.q: What happens to God's blessing after Abraham dies?

options.text: God blesses Isaac, so the covenant favour continues to the next generation.
options.note: Verse 11 shows the blessing passing on; the promise does not die with Abraham.

options.text: The blessing ends with Abraham's death.
options.note: The opposite; the text stresses that God then blessed Isaac.

options.text: The blessing is divided among all Abraham's sons.
options.note: The blessing rests on Isaac specifically, not on all the sons.

options.text: The blessing passes to Ishmael as the elder son.
options.note: God blesses Isaac, the son of promise, not Ishmael.

quiz.q: What does Abraham's contented death teach about living by God's promise?

options.text: One can die satisfied by faith even having seen only the beginnings of what God pledged.
options.note: Abraham rests in God's faithfulness though full fulfilment lay ahead.

options.text: God's promises must be fully seen in this life or faith fails.
options.note: Abraham died before full fulfilment yet contented; faith rests in God, not in complete sight.

options.text: A long life is proof that one has pleased God.
options.note: His contentment rests on God's faithfulness, not merely on length of days.

options.text: The promise depended on Abraham staying alive.
options.note: The blessing passes to Isaac; the promise outlasts Abraham's life.

questions: Abraham died old and contented, at peace with God and his family. What would it take for you to be able to say your life is satisfied in God?
The inheritance went to Isaac, the son of promise, by God's design. Where do you need to trust God's choices even when they differ from human expectation?
Two estranged brothers, Isaac and Ishmael, buried their father together. Is there a broken relationship where God might be inviting you toward peace?
God's blessing did not die with Abraham but passed to Isaac. How does it encourage you that God's purposes are bigger than any single life, including your own?
Abraham was gathered to his people in hope. How does the resurrection of Christ shape the way you think about your own death and those you have lost?

translationNotes.note: The phrase gathered to his people is distinct from being buried in the next verse, and suggests joining one's forebears, an early hint of hope beyond death.
The sons of the concubines refers to children of Keturah and Hagar; they are provided for but set apart from Isaac, the covenant heir.
